g11-geography-ug3-t1.overview: Land is the ultimate resource and the foundation of all human activity. This lesson examines the importance and functions of land, classifies its resources, and explains how land management keeps exploitation and regeneration in balance.
objectives: Explain the importance of land as a natural resource from different perspectives
Classify land resources by regeneration, origin, availability, distribution and stage of development
Identify the functions of land as a resource and as an environment
Define land management and state its prime objective
Describe practical land management practices used to protect soil, water and vegetation
g11-geography-ug3-t1.simple: Land is a very broad concept. It can be viewed as a resource, an environment, a legal object, an economic asset and cultural wealth. Because land is the ultimate resource, life on Earth cannot be sustained without it. From land we obtain food, shelter, space to work and room to relax. Its resources come from the lithosphere, biosphere, atmosphere and hydrosphere, and are classified as renewable or non-renewable, biotic or abiotic, stock or flow, and potential, actual or conditional. Renewable resources replace themselves only if the rate of use is less than the rate of regeneration, so even renewables can be exhausted by excessive use. Non-renewable resources such as minerals and fossil fuels exist in finite supply and must be managed carefully through recycling and reuse. Land management is the proper use and protection of land resources; its prime objective is to control land degradation.
g11-geography-ug3-t1.detailed:
Why land is the ultimate resource. Land is a very broad concept with a wider range of meanings. It can be examined as a resource, an environment, a legal object, an economic asset and/or cultural wealth. It is the ultimate resource and the foundation of all forms of human activity: without it, life on Earth cannot be sustained. It is the source of all wealth, and it is both a physical commodity and an abstract concept, because the rights to own or use it are as much a part of the land as the object rooted in the soil. From the land we obtain food, shelter, space to work and room to relax.

Classifying land resources. Land resources are useable materials occurring naturally in the environment. They are derived from the Earth, coming from the Lithosphere, Biosphere, Atmosphere or Hydrosphere. They are classified by: regeneration (renewable and non-renewable); origin (biotic and abiotic); current use and future availability (stock and flow resources); distribution and volume (ubiquitous, unique, common and rare resources); and stage of development (potential, actual and conditional resources).

Renewable resources. Plants and animals are regenerative and replaceable after use, as long as the rate of use is less than the rate of regeneration and their environments are well kept. Renewable resources can be replenished or reproduced easily, but the rate of regeneration differs: crops take a short time to regenerate, soil may take a relatively long time, and forest resources take longer than others. Even so, many renewable resources can be depleted through excessive use - being renewable does not mean they can never be exhausted. Some must be used wisely; sustainable (wise) use is the basic requirement for preserving land resources. A few renewables are inexhaustible flow resources, such as sunlight, oxygen in the atmosphere and wind.

Non-renewable resources. These exist in a finite supply and do not replace themselves after use; they diminish in size and quality with excessive use. Minerals and fossil fuels are the best examples. Their rate of formation is very slow, so once depleted they cannot be replenished soon. Because they are difficult to get back, recycling and reusing are among the recommended management options. Reuse means using a resource over and over again, in the same form or after recycling. However, coal and petroleum cannot be recycled the way metallic minerals can, so unmanaged use may cause rapid exhaustion and restrict the benefit of coming generations.

Land as an environment and its functions. As an environment, land is an area of the Earth's surface embracing all biotic and abiotic components on, above and below the surface: plants and animals of the biosphere, atmospheric gases, underlying geology and soils, hydrology, and the results of past and present human activities. As a usable material, land serves several functions: a production function (a means of production), a waste disposal function (a sink of wastes), an economic asset (it can be converted into a capital resource), and a cultural asset (the host of traditional and religious sacred amenities). Ecologically, land plays a vital role in the breeding and survival of living organisms.

Land management. Land management is the proper use and protection of land resources to provide optimal benefit to growing populations and uphold sustained ecosystem services. Managed land should deliver food and fiber, distinctive landscape opportunities for outdoor public recreation, and pivotal ecological functions. It must protect wider landscapes and resources - mountains, hills, rivers, depressions, water, air, vegetation and wildlife - and reflect the principles of sustainable resource use, building on national, regional and local needs. The prime objective of land management is to control land degradation to balance resource exploitation and regeneration. In practice it rests on managing soil, water, natural vegetation and air: proper farming practices, tree planting (afforestation and reforestation), controlled grazing, terracing and check-damming protect soils, water and forests, while fuel-saving technologies in vehicles and renewable power sources such as hydropower reduce environmental pollution. Because land management is materialized through protecting resources, it should also consider cultural, economic and political settings, rely on indigenous culture and local knowledge, and educate the immediate beneficiaries.

workedExamples.problem: A student lists four resources found in a village in southern Ethiopia: Maize crops, forest cedar trees, soil, and sunshine. Using the concept of rate of regeneration, place them from fastest to slowest to regenerate and say what this implies for use.
workedExamples.given: The textbook states crops take a short time to regenerate, soil may take a relatively long time, and forest resources take longer than others.
workedExamples.formula: Concept: the rate of regeneration differs from resource to resource and limits how fast each can be used.
workedExamples.substitution: Ordering the four: crops (short), forest trees (long), soil (relatively long), sunlight (inexhaustible flow, not consumed up).
workedExamples.calculation: Resources used faster than their regeneration rate are depleted even though they are renewable; sunlight is a flow resource that renews continuously.
workedExamples.answer: Fastest to slowest: crops, then forest trees and soil, with sunlight inexhaustible; each resource must be used only at or below its regeneration rate.

workedExamples.problem: A learner argues that a forest can never be exhausted because it is a renewable resource. Evaluate the claim against the textbook definition.
workedExamples.given: Renewable resources replace themselves as far as the rate of use is less than the rate of regeneration.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: being renewable does not mean never depleting; excessive use can exhaust any renewable resource.
workedExamples.substitution: If cutting for fuel and farmland clearing exceeds tree regrowth, the forest stock shrinks each year.
workedExamples.calculation: The claim fails the renewal test, since use above the regeneration rate makes the forest non-sustaining.
workedExamples.answer: The claim is wrong: renewable resources can be easily depleted if excessively used, so wise use is the basic requirement for preserving them.

workedExamples.problem: A country relies heavily on its coal and petroleum reserves. The textbooks recommend recycling and reusing for non-renewables. Can coal and petroleum be protected in the same way as metallic minerals? Explain.
workedExamples.given: Coal and petroleum cannot be recycled like metallic minerals.
workedExamples.formula: Concept: management options for non-renewables depend on whether the resource can be physically recycled.
workedExamples.substitution: Metallic minerals can be melted and reprocessed; burned fuels become gases and wastes that cannot be reprocessed.
workedExamples.calculation: Since recycling is not possible for coal and petroleum, the only workable option is to carefully manage and reduce their use, or the resource will be rapidly exhausted.
workedExamples.answer: No. Coal and petroleum cannot be recycled, so they require careful management of use to avoid rapid exhaustion and restricted benefits to future generations.

workedExamples.problem: Match each land use problem in a district with the land management practice the textbook suggests: (a) soil loss on steep slopes, (b) vegetation removal by grazing animals, (c) home cooking demand for firewood.
workedExamples.given: Practices named in the lesson: terracing, controlled grazing, afforestation and reforestation, check-damming, proper farming.
workedExamples.formula: Method: each physical problem has a matching conservation practice.
workedExamples.substitution: (a) Steep slopes and running water - terracing; (b) Grazing pressure - controlled grazing; (c) Fuel demand - tree planting and renewable power such as hydropower.
workedExamples.calculation: Terracing reduces the force of running water, controlled grazing spares vegetation, and planting plus renewable energy cuts the firewood burden on forests.
workedExamples.answer: (a) Terracing; (b) Controlled grazing; (c) Afforestation/reforestation supported by renewable energy sources.

g11-geography-ug3-t2.overview: Soils, water and forests are common-pool resources placed under immense pressure by rapid population growth and migration. This lesson examines how each is degraded and the measures that can reduce the pressure.
objectives: Identify the renewable resources that face the greatest human pressure
Explain the concept of common-pool resources and the tragedy of the commons
Describe the causes and forms of soil degradation
Explain the pressures and future risks facing freshwater resources
Evaluate measures to protect water resources and forest resources
g11-geography-ug3-t2.simple: All environmental resources are affected by excessive human use, but soils, water and forests are the most influenced and placed under increased pressure. Large parts of these resources are common-pool wealth, so they are repeatedly misused, mismanaged and degraded - a situation known as the tragedy of the commons. Nearly 33% of the world's arable land has been destroyed by soil erosion, through lost nutrients, removal of topsoil, crusting and compaction, and pollution. Freshwater suffers from pollution by wastes, plastic bags and water hyacinth, and scarcity now affects many arid areas of the Middle East, Africa and Asia. About 13 million hectares of forest are converted to other uses each year. Remedies include erosion control, safe sewerage, watershed management, afforestation such as Ethiopia's Green Legacy, and alternative renewable energy sources.
g11-geography-ug3-t2.detailed:
Common-pool resources under pressure. Of all renewable resources, soils, water and forests are the most influenced by humans and face increased pressure. Large parts of them exist as common-pool wealth in many areas and face greater pressure, known as the tragedy of the commons: because nobody holds exclusive responsibility, they are repeatedly misused, mismanaged and degraded through unwise and careless use. They face the prime impact of rapid population growth and increased rural-urban migration.

Soil resources. Soils are essential agricultural resources, but they lose their intrinsic quality through erosion or excessive utilization. Nearly 33% of the world's arable land and soils has been destroyed by soil erosion (assessed by GLASOD, the Global Assessment of Human-induced Soil Degradation, 1990). The main causes of depletion are loss of essential soil nutrients, reduction of biological components, removal of the topsoil, crusting and compaction, plus pollution and soil salinity. Soil degradation takes three forms: physical (crusting, compaction, depth reduction), chemical (salinization, alkalinisation, acidification), and biological (loss of soil biota and decline of soil organic carbon). Depletion reduces productive capacity and environmental quality and annihilates essential ecosystem functions. Solutions exist: proper utilization, adoption of erosion control structures, and the addition of manure and natural fertilizers.

Water resources. Water is a basic life necessity for people and animals, essential for plant growth, soil formation, rock weathering, organic matter decomposition and rainfall formation, and it serves as a habitat for diverse life forms and as a producer of power. Yet at the start of the 21st century freshwater fell under greater pressure from more directions than ever before in Earth's history. Rivers and lakes near urban areas are polluted by domestic and industrial wastes, plastic bags and exotic water plants like the water hyacinth; oil spills from steamships and boats, and chemicals released from industries, cause excessive accumulation of nutrients and toxicity in lakes and rivers. Water scarcity is distressing many arid and semi-arid areas where population pressure is extensive, including parts of the Middle East, Africa and Asia. With world population likely to approach 10 billion by 2050, demand from agriculture and industry will rise, and pollution of surface and ground waters will reduce freshwater quality; climate change may upset the hydrological cycle. The feared outcome is a worldwide water crisis in the middle of this century, and water may emerge as a source of contention between nations sharing river basins.

Measures to sustain freshwater. The textbook lists measures that address competing uses: developing safe waste disposal sewerage systems, especially in urban areas, to keep domestic effluents from streams and lakes; adopting laws restricting the withdrawal of wastes to river and lake systems; locating industries far from rivers and lakes; desalination of sea water to minimize stress on streams and lakes; recycling waste water through careful treatment; using porous pavements so wastewater does not drain from impervious urban surfaces into watercourses; and watershed management.

Forest resources. Forests constitute the largest terrestrial ecosystems and donate subsistence items, income and agricultural inputs to billions of people, while providing services like climate stabilization, flood control, waste filtration and soil erosion control, storing the world's carbon stocks, and serving as habitat for the Earth's known terrestrial species. Nevertheless, deforestation, encroachment of farming into communal forest areas and mismanagement greatly reduce these services. About 13 million hectares of forested lands have been converted annually into other land uses at the global level over the past few decades. Forest clearance for large-scale plantation agriculture and livestock ranching in the tropics, for example in the Amazon basin, has destroyed rainforest ecosystems, while biofuel demand, mining, rapid urbanization, climate change and changing consumption patterns add pressure.

Protecting forests and pressured non-renewables. Measures to safeguard forest security include initiating afforestation and reforestation programs like the Green Legacy practiced in Ethiopia; integrating forest management with Soil and Water Conservation (SWC) programs; seeking alternative energy from other renewables such as hydropower, solar power and wind power; adopting restrictive laws and bylaws on unwise use of common-pool forests; encouraging participatory forest management that engages users in decision making; education and awareness creation; and watershed management. Among non-renewable resources, fossil fuels (natural oil and coal) and precious minerals (gold and diamonds) face intense pressure, and their exploitation has frequently caused conflict among ethnic groups and between countries, for example in the Middle East, Central Africa and West Africa.

workedExamples.problem: A district cropland of 90,000 hectares has followed the global pattern stated in the textbook: nearly 33% of the world's arable land has been destroyed by soil erosion. How many hectares would that represent, and how many remain healthy?

workedExamples.problem: Match each freshwater problem with its recommended measure: (a) urban domestic effluents entering a lake, (b) an industry discharging beside a river bank, (c) excessive evaporation loss of usable water in a coastal town.

g11-geography-ug3-t3.overview: Resource degradation is the overall loss of the quality and quantity of land resources, driven by underlying and proximate causes. This lesson traces the causes and consequences of degradation and the conservation measures that check it.
objectives: Define resource degradation and name its human and natural triggers
Distinguish underlying causes from proximate causes of land degradation
Describe the consequences of degradation for people and ecosystems
Identify physical conservation structures and soil improvement practices
Explain how degradation links to poverty, food insecurity and migration
g11-geography-ug3-t3.simple: Resource degradation is the overall loss or decline of the quality and quantity of land resources such as soils, water and biological mass. It is often initiated by human activity, and sometimes by natural hazards like earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, landslides and flooding. Degradation happens worldwide but hits developing countries like those in Africa hardest. Its causes split into underlying sources, such as rapid population growth, climate change, rough topography, improper land use and poor policy, and proximate causes they produce, such as intensive land use, deforestation and overgrazing. Consequences include loss of soil productivity, biodiversity loss, desertification, low agricultural yields, hunger, poverty and migration. Degradation can be checked through land management practices: afforestation, reforestation, area closures, terracing, check dams, mulching, shelterbelts, trenches, legume rotation and the addition of manure.
g11-geography-ug3-t3.detailed:
The concept of degradation. Resource degradation is the overall loss (decline) of the quality and quantity of land resources such as soils, water and biological mass. It is often initiated by human activity and sometimes by natural hazards such as earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, landsliding and flooding. Degraded land appears worldwide: the textbook photographs degraded land in the Atsbi-Womberta area, Tigray, Ethiopia, an eroded wasteland in Rajasthan (India), erosion on a cotton plantation farm in Ghana, and eroded 'badlands' over sodic soils in Bolivia. Although degradation happens at a wider scale all over the world, its impacts are much worse in developing countries like those in Africa. It is commonly connected with climate change and widespread poverty.

Underlying causes. Sources of land resource degradation are categorized as underlying and proximate causes. The underlying sources are major causes that promote proximate issues to happen. They include rapid population growth, climate change (decreasing rainfalls and increasing temperatures), rough topography (steep slopes and depressions), improper land use practices and government policy, especially poor tenure policy that creates tenure insecurity.

Proximate causes. The proximate causes are secondary issues initiated by the underlying agents. Rapid population growth raises the demand for food and farmland, producing intensive use of land, farmland fragmentation, repeated tillage and depletion of soil fertility. More demand for biomass energy and timber leads to deforestation and forest cover contraction. More demand for pasture and livestock feed produces overstocking and overgrazing, which uproot and remove vegetation. Climate change brings desertification - contraction of vegetation cover, decreasing crop harvest and poverty. Sudden, unprecedented and torrential rainfalls cause flooding, leading to soil and biodiversity losses and to sedimentation and siltation of dams and reservoirs. Steep slopes speed up stream flow so soil is removed from upper catchments, while depressions cause waterlogging, soil acidity and cultivation difficulties. Poor farming methods such as ploughing up and down slopes remove soil from farmlands, and poor land management - less use of fallowing, crop rotation and animal manure plus excessive irrigation - brings loss of soil nutrients, fertility depletion and salinization.

Consequences. Rapid population growth and technological advances over the past 50 years have changed land use worldwide: forest covers have decreased, cultivated lands increased, rain-fed areas expanded, irrigated areas have doubled, and permanent meadows and pastures grew. A significant proportion of the world's arable land was destroyed by soil erosion, and the per capita farmland needed to feed people declined. Land resource degradation could finally result in: loss of biodiversity (reduction of animal and plant populations), desertification of local environments, low levels of agricultural yields and animal production, worsened hunger and poverty, food insecurity and migration, and a lessened capacity of the land to function within the ecological system.

Structural conservation measures. Depletion and degradation can be checked through land management practices. Afforestation plants trees on barren lands that were not under forest cover before; reforestation replants trees in deforested areas; area closures close deforested areas from livestock contact to restore the previous status; terracing constructs bench terraces on steep lands to reduce the force of running water and trap moving soil; a check dam is a small or temporary structure built across a waterway to control erosion by reducing water flow velocity, important for conserving gullied areas; mulching covers soil with plant residue so the soil regains nutrients as the residue decays and loses less water to evaporation; and shelterbelts plant trees along lines to break the speed of blowing wind and reduce its erosivity. Other structures include diversion canals to divert upcoming floods from farmlands, trenches to trap down-going water and soil, and drainage channels (ditches) to remove excess water from depressed areas. The textbook illustrates these with stone Bunds in the May-Leiba catchment in Tigray, terrace structures over the loess hill slopes of China, a restored gully in Awzet, Farta, Ethiopia, and restored forest land in Nepal.

Agronomic measures. Natural and farming measures complement the structures: legume-rotation to replenish soil fertility; the addition of animal manure to replace lost nutrients; inter-cropping to augment soil fertility; proper irrigation to minimize soil salinity; the addition of chemical fertilizer to replace lost nutrients; and using green manure to uphold soil fertility. Future improvement of rural livelihoods and income levels depends largely on the rational use of available resources and increased application of agricultural technologies.

g11-geography-ug3-t4.overview: More than 263 transboundary watercourses criss-cross 145 nations and support about 40% of the global population. This lesson maps their distribution and shows why shared rivers bring both prospects for cooperation and risks of conflict.
objectives: Define transboundary rivers and transboundary waters

g11-geography-ug3-t4.simple: Transboundary rivers are watercourses shared by two or more countries. Together with transboundary lakes, inland waters and aquifers, they are called transboundary waters; oceans, territorial seas and coastal waters are not included. More than 263 transnational river and lake channels, plus numerous trans-border aquifers, are known to geographers. They make up around 60% of the world's freshwater flows and cover nearly half of the Earth's terrestrial surface, passing through 145 nations and supporting about 40% of the world's people. About 60% of Africa's and South America's space falls under inter-state rivers. Shared waters provide ecosystem services - food, shelter for aquatic life, flood and pollution control - and build hydrological, social and economic integration, yet they can also become sources of conflict among riparian countries, as Ethiopia and Egypt show over the Nile.
g11-geography-ug3-t4.detailed:
What transboundary waters are. Transboundary rivers are watercourses shared by two or more countries. Together with lakes, inland waters and aquifers, they are named 'transboundary waters'; oceans, territorial seas and coastal waters are not included in this category. Worldwide, more than 263 transnational river and lake channels plus numerous trans-state aquifers are currently known to geographers. These 263 watercourses make up around 60% of the world's freshwater flows and cover nearly one-half of the Earth's terrestrial surface. They pass across the terrains of 145 nations and support about 40% of the global population.

Regional patterns. About 60% of the space of Africa and South America and nearly 40% of North and Central America fall under inter-state rivers. Around 80% of the total area of 44 countries lies within international basins: twenty of these are in Africa, thirteen in Europe, seven in Asia and four in Latin America. The entire area of some 30 countries falls within trans-state waters, and a total of 21 countries lie entirely within international basins. Groundwaters interlinked with about 300 transboundary aquifers also support nearly two million people around the world.

Shared basins by the numbers. There are 13 basins worldwide shared between five and eight riparian states. Five basins - the Congo, Niger, Nile, Rhine and Zambezi - are shared between nine and eleven states. The river flowing through the most nations is the Danube, which travels through the territory of 19 nations. Sample basins in the textbook's table show how varied shared rivers are: the Nile rises from Lake Victoria, drains 3,030,700 square kilometres, delivers 84 billion cubic meters (BCM) annually, has 11 riparian countries, and runs 6,671 kilometres to the Mediterranean Sea; the Congo carries 1,250 BCM to the Atlantic Ocean; the Zambezi (source in Zambia) delivers 230 BCM to the Indian Ocean through 8 riparian countries; the Amazon (source in the Andes Mountains) covers 6,800,000 square kilometres across 9 riparian countries and flows 6,400 kilometres; and the Jordan, rising from Mount Hermon between Syria and Lebanon, is only 360 kilometres long with a flow of 540 million cubic meters per year, emptying into the Dead Sea with 5 riparian countries.

Prospects of shared rivers. Internationally shared waters connect populations of diverse countries and support the revenues and livelihoods of millions of people. Shared wetlands, lakes and floodplains provide priceless ecosystem services: food, shelter for aquatic life, and control of flooding and pollution. They create hydrological, social and economic integrations among people and countries, and they can play a great role in socioeconomic development and help reduce poverty. Shared rivers also provide prospects for collaboration and improvement of regional peace and security in addition to socioeconomic growth.

The other side: impacts and conflict. Exhausted, despoiled, poorly developed and unmanaged freshwater courses that result from rapid population increase may impede sustainable development and hinder partnership between main water-use segments such as agriculture, industry, energy, navigation, water supply and sanitation. Inter-state collaborations and partnerships are the best options to address diverging interests over shared basins. Nevertheless, shared watercourses appear to be sources of both conflict and dialogue among countries despite their implanted potential for cooperation - like the case of Ethiopia and Egypt over the use of the Nile waters.

Economic uses along the rivers. Dams and economic projects over the Nile Basin listed in the textbook include Roseires in Sudan; the Aswan High Dam in Egypt; Owen Falls Dam in Uganda; and in Ethiopia the Tekeze hydroelectric power (HEP) project, Tana Beles, Tis Abay, the Fincha dam and Koga irrigation, plus the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD). Elsewhere in Africa, the Zambezi carries Victoria Falls and the Congo River runs the hydroelectric dam at Inga Falls, while the Niger supports fishing. Such waters serve fishing, transportation, development, offshore oilfields and culture - and could all become sources of conflict if not handled wisely.

g11-geography-ug3-t5.overview: Because shared basins cross many jurisdictions with different priorities, riparian states need organizing agreements and regional institutions. This lesson evaluates why cooperation matters and surveys the institutions that manage shared rivers.
objectives: Explain why regional cooperation is needed for the sustainable use of shared rivers
Appraise the role of regional institutions in preventing water use conflicts
Identify major river-based organizations and their member states
Interpret statistics on bilateral and multilateral water conventions
Evaluate the objectives of the Nile Basin Initiative
g11-geography-ug3-t5.simple: Rivers and lakes frequently pass across numerous governmental and jurisdictional confines whose holders have diverse priorities, intentions and interests. Because of political and institutional complications, the shared resources of a single basin cannot be managed rationally on a long-term basis without some organizing agreement and governing rule among the riparian states. Research shows plenty of institutions and treaties now govern rights, responsibilities and duties over shared watercourses: of the 263 shared basins of the world, 176 (67%) had bilateral conventions. For a rational thinker, conflict and war never benefit riparian states; formal interstate cooperation does. Examples include the Nile Basin Initiative, the Lesotho Highlands Development Authority, the Zambezi River Authority, the Kagera Basin Organization, the Southern African Power Pool, SARCCUS and the US-Canada International Joint Commission.
g11-geography-ug3-t5.detailed:
Why cooperation is necessary. Rivers and lakes frequently cross numerous governmental and jurisdictional confines that typically have diverse priorities, intentions and interests. The issue becomes more intricate when two or more countries are involved. Because of political and/or institutional complications, the shared resources of a single basin cannot be managed rationally on a long-term basis. This implies that some form of organizing agreement must be considered between the riparian states, and some form of governing rule is required to harmonize relations between riparian societies and organizations - to achieve effective water use and management that maximizes human welfare and safeguards the environment.

Institutions prevent disputes. Some people argue that shared watercourses would be major sources of conflict and war between countries. But, for rational thinkers, conflicts and wars never benefit riparian states; they benefit more through inter-state formal cooperation. National, regional or international institutions are therefore considered basic components for the alleviation of potential disputes arising from the use of shared watercourses. Research shows plenty of institutions and treaties today focus on the rights, responsibilities and duties of countries sharing specific international watercourses.

Bilateral and multilateral treaties. Of the 263 shared basins of the world, 176 (67%) had bilateral conventions. Nevertheless, 79% of the covenants of the past were in watercourses crossing three or more riparian countries, and most joint covenants from multilateral basins were also of bilateral type (a 2:1 relation). This indicates that many of the agreements were intentionally excluding one or more riparian countries within a given catchment - a problem especially felt by downstream-ignored upstream states like Ethiopia in the Nile basin.

The Nile Basin Initiative (NBI). The NBI grew from a pact created to coordinate Nile basin resource management and socio-economic development in the riparian states. It was initiated in December 1992 with the creation of a Technical Cooperation Committee for the Promotion of Development and Environmental Protection of the Nile Basin (TECCONILE), first initiated by six Nile River riparian states: Egypt, Sudan, Rwanda, Uganda, Tanzania and Zaire. Ethiopia, Kenya, Eritrea and Burundi were observers at the initial time. Between 1997 and 2001 considerable progress was made in designing structures and institutions for a new basin regime, and TECCONILE was replaced by the NBI in 1999. The NBI was first signed by Ministers of Water Resources of the riparian states on 22 February 1999 in Dar-es-Salaam, Tanzania. Its main objectives were to promote sustainable socio-economic development in the basin states, equitable utilization and benefit of the basin resources, recognition of the rights of all riparian states, and an inclusive legal framework (the Nile Task) for equitable and sustainable allocation of Nile waters and resources.

African river-basin organizations. The Lesotho Highlands Development Authority (LHDA) was created by Lesotho and the Republic of South Africa by a treaty signed in 1986 to transfer water from the head-reaches of the Orange River to the key industrial areas of the RSA in the Pretoria-Witwatersrand-Vereeniging region; a Joint Permanent Technical Commission (JPTC) plus the LHDA in Lesotho and the Trans-Caledon Tunnel Authority (TCTA) in the RSA implement the project. The Zambezi River Authority (ZRA) is a bilateral river basin organization between Zambia and Zimbabwe whose objectives are to operate and maintain the Kariba dam, investigate new projects, and collect data linked with national utilities. The Kagera Basin Organization (KBO) was created in 1977 by Burundi, Rwanda and Tanzania, later joined by Uganda in 1981, to strengthen cooperation through joint planning and development of sub-regional potentials. The Southern African Power Pool (SAPP), created in 1995, serves a twelve-country region (Angola, Botswana, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Swaziland, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe) with large cheap hydroelectric reserves in the north (principally the Inga reservoir), large low-cost coal deposits in the RSA, and the Kariba Dam on the Zambia-Zimbabwe border playing the buffer role. SARCCUS (Southern African Regional Commission for the Conservation and Utilization of the Soil) coordinates the conservation of water and soils on shared river basins among South African countries.

Beyond Africa. The US-Canada International Joint Commission (IJC) is an international institution working on water management in the Great Lakes region of North America, created by the Waters Treaty signed between the USA and Canada in 1909. It works not only on water sharing but also on the lakes' environmental management and pollution control, and it is cited as successful in resolving all transboundary issues referred to it - proof that well-built institutional cooperation can hold a basin together for over a century.

g11-geography-ug3-t6.overview: Ethiopia, Sudan and Egypt share the Nile, but the water they use differs sharply from the water they possess. This lesson compares potential and actual water use of the three countries and shows how colonial-era treaties still shape the dispute.
objectives: Compare the actual per capita water use of Ethiopia, Sudan and Egypt
Define the WHO water availability threshold and apply it
Describe the historical ties among the three countries
Summarize the major Nile treaties from 1929 and 1959
Explain why the 1959 treaty is contested although most of the Nile's water flows from Ethiopia
g11-geography-ug3-t6.simple: Ethiopia, Sudan and Egypt are African countries sharing several socioeconomic, cultural and natural resources. Ethiopia and Egypt exchanged popes for their Orthodox churches through long history, and Ethiopia and Sudan share a long land border plus strong economic ties. All three share the Nile water. Actual per capita water use is about 1,666 cubic meters per person per year in Ethiopia, around 1,981 cubic meters in Sudan, and only about 830 cubic meters in Egypt - below the 1,700 cubic meters per person per annum proposed by the World Health Organization. Although the Nile is shared by 11 riparian states and its basin supports over 160 million people, past hydropower and irrigation use was dominated by Egypt and Sudan through treaties like those of 1929 and 1959, while upstream countries, including Ethiopia, were left out.
g11-geography-ug3-t6.detailed:
Three neighbors, one river. Ethiopia, Sudan and Egypt share several socioeconomic, cultural and natural resources and have experienced similar culture, religion and even economic characteristics through their long history. Ethiopia and Egypt exchanged popes for their Orthodox Churches in the past; Ethiopia and Sudan share a long land border plus strong economic ties; and the three countries together share the Nile water and its resources. Yet they sometimes appear to experience conflicts among themselves: the sources of conflict originate from the land and water resources shared among them, and the main cause emanates from the utilization and development of the Nile waters.

Actual use compared with the WHO standard. Actual per capita water use differs sharply: in Ethiopia about 1,666 cubic meters per person per year; in Sudan about 1,981 cubic meters per person per annum; and in Egypt only about 830 cubic meters per person per year. Egypt's figure is below the 1,700 cubic meters per person per annum proposed by the World Health Organization (WHO) - meaning that despite its historic grip on the Nile, Egypt lives under severe per-capita water scarcity, which intensifies its sensitivity to any new upstream use.

The Nile and its users. The Nile River is shared by 11 riparian countries. The basin supports over 160 million people, while the total population of the riparian states is estimated at over 300 million. Yet the use of Nile waters for hydropower generation and irrigation was in the past exclusively dominated by Egypt and Sudan; widespread poverty and lingering political instability hindered upstream countries from effectively using the potential of the Nile. This mismatch between origin and use is the heart of the conflict: the great majority of the Nile water flows from Ethiopia, while the great share of its consumption happens downstream.

The 1929 treaty. On 7 May 1929, an 'Exchange of Notes' on the re-use of the waters of the River Nile for irrigation was signed between the United Kingdom and Egypt. Egypt claimed 'natural and historic rights' over the Nile waters, and the United Kingdom recognized Egypt's 'natural and historic rights in the waters of the Nile'. In 1952 Egypt and the UK exchanged notes on the Owen Falls Dam and Aswan High Dam proposal, the Aswan High Dam being proposed with 156 BCM per year of storage capacity. On 8 November 1954 Egypt demanded a share of additional water from Sudan, and that first round of negotiations ended inconclusively.

The 1959 treaty. On 8 November 1959, Egypt and Sudan signed a treaty for the full utilization of the Nile waters and created a Permanent Joint Technical Commission. Under it, all Nile water was distributed between just the two countries: Egypt was granted 55.5 BCM and Sudan 18.5 BCM, with the rest left for losses from evaporation and seepage. Ethiopia was not a party. As the unit summary stresses, Ethiopia will never be forced to accept the treaty signed in her absence, and the right of Ethiopia was deliberately overlooked in the 1959 treaty - which is why Ethiopia contests it and argues it has no obligation to abide by it.

Later developments. Later conventions confirmed the intention to cooperate on Nile waters and to refrain from engaging in activities that cause appreciable harm to the interests of others; cooperation on sustainable development of the basin led to the creation of the Lake Victoria Basin Commission; and the signing of the Cooperative Framework Agreement (CFA) was designed to create a permanent Nile River Basin Commission based on common understanding, mutual benefit, good faith, win-win cooperation and principles of international law. Sudan and Egypt nowadays challenge the construction of the GERD (Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam), saying it might affect their water supply, and they often argue Ethiopia should abide by the 1959 agreement; Ethiopia replies that the 1959 treaty allotted nothing to Ethiopia at all.

workedExamples.problem: Using the per capita figures, compare Ethiopia's, Sudan's and Egypt's annual water use per person and identify which country falls short of the WHO proposal.
workedExamples.given: Ethiopia 1,666 m3 per person per year; Sudan 1,981 m3; Egypt 830 m3; WHO proposes 1,700 m3 per person per annum.
workedExamples.formula: Method: subtraction against the 1,700 m3 benchmark to find the gap.
workedExamples.substitution: Ethiopia: 1,700 - 1,666 = 34 m3 above the minimum; Sudan: 1,981 - 1,700 = 281 m3 above; Egypt: 1,700 - 830 = 870 m3 short.
workedExamples.calculation: Ethiopia barely clears the threshold while Egypt falls far below it, about half the benchmark.
workedExamples.answer: Egypt's per capita use (about 830 m3) is the only one below the WHO's 1,700 m3, which explains its acute sensitivity over the Nile.

workedExamples.problem: How many BCM of Nile water were distributed by the 1959 treaty, and how much was left for losses?
workedExamples.given: The 1959 treaty granted Egypt 55.5 BCM and Sudan 18.5 BCM; the rest was left for losses from evaporation and seepage.
workedExamples.formula: Method: sum the allocated volumes and subtract from the basin's annual flow.
workedExamples.substitution: 55.5 + 18.5 = 74 BCM allocated to Egypt and Sudan combined.
workedExamples.calculation: Deducting 74 BCM from the approximate annual flow of 84 BCM stated in the basin table leaves about 10 BCM counted for evaporation and seepage losses.
workedExamples.answer: 74 BCM was split between Egypt (55.5) and Sudan (18.5), with almost everything else written off as evaporation and seepage - and nothing for Ethiopia.

workedExamples.problem: Ethiopia argues it is not bound by the 1959 treaty. Build the geographic argument from the data.
workedExamples.given: Over 85% of the Nile water flows from Ethiopia; the 1959 treaty was signed in Ethiopia's absence; Egypt was granted 55.5 BCM and Sudan 18.5 BCM; Ethiopia received no share.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: fairness of allocation should relate water origin and basin population to shares.
workedExamples.substitution: The biggest contributor (Ethiopia) signed nothing and was allotted nothing, while non-contributing allocations went fully to downstream states.
workedExamples.calculation: A treaty signed in a country's absence cannot bind it under basic international principles of sovereignty as stated in the unit summary.
workedExamples.answer: Ethiopia will not be forced to accept a treaty signed in her absence and whose allocation deliberately overlooked her rights - hence the continuing contention over use and development of Nile water.

workedExamples.problem: The Nile basin supports over 160 million people while the riparian states total over 300 million. What does this gap indicate about pressure on the river?
workedExamples.given: Basin population: over 160 million; total riparian-state population: over 300 million; actual irrigation and hydropower use historically dominated by Egypt and Sudan.
workedExamples.formula: Concept: basin population concentrates directly on the water resource, while state-wide population could spill into basins and raise demand.
workedExamples.substitution: About half of the three countries' wider populations already live inside the Nile basin; the other half can migrate in and raise demand.
workedExamples.calculation: Meet that with upstream countries being too poor and unstable to use the river, and the pressure argues for cooperative, not exclusive, use.
workedExamples.answer: Half of all riparian-state people depend directly on one basin dominated by two downstream users - a formula for rising demand and future contention unless use becomes equitable.

g11-geography-ug3-t7.overview: When the size of natural resources shrinks, asset scarcity triggers disputes over access, control and use - the natural resource conflict. This lesson examines the concept, causes, forms, actors and resolution strategies of such conflicts worldwide.
objectives: Define natural resource conflict and explain how scarcity triggers it
Identify the four kinds of resource conflicts recognized as challenges to national stability
Give concrete examples of conflicts over water, land, timber, fuel and minerals
List the conditions under which resource conflicts arise and their forms of expression
Compare the six basic strategies people use to handle conflicts
g11-geography-ug3-t7.simple: Natural resources are useable assets essential for human livelihoods, and access to them partly decides the wealth and prestige of people and even the position of countries in the international economic system. Some resources, like diamonds, minerals and natural oil, are exhaustible: their market value rises as their quantities shrink, and the resulting asset scarcity triggers conflict among users - what is commonly called a natural resource conflict. Over the past six decades some 40-60% of civil wars were instigated by the control and use of natural resources. Conflicts arise over water and pasture, land, timber, fuel and minerals, and they are handled through strategies such as negotiation, arbitration, mediation and adjudication, or worsened through avoidance and coercion.
g11-geography-ug3-t7.detailed:
The concept of resource conflict. Resource conflicts are disputes arising over accessing, controlling and using materials found in nature. People use resources such as forests, water, pastures and land, so disputes often emerge from them. Conflicts also arise when the interests and needs of users are not met, or when the priorities of some user groups are not considered by governments. Such conflicts of interest are inevitable features of all societies, and in recent years their scope and magnitude have increased and intensified. If not addressed, they can escalate into violence and cause environmental degradation and deterioration of livelihoods; recognizing conflicts, however, is a prerequisite for sustainable management and equitable use.

Scarcity and market value. Access to natural resources partly decides the wealth and prestige of people and even the position of countries in the international economic system. Resources like diamonds, minerals and natural oil are available in limited amounts and can be exhausted with use. The market value of such resources rises when their quantities shrink. When the size of natural resources shrinks, asset scarcity occurs, and the shortage triggers conflict among the resource users. The textbook warns that some 40-60% of the civil wars of the past six decades were instigated by the control and use of natural resources, especially in countries with weak administration, high levels of corruption and fierce ethnic and political divisions. Yet grievances over shared resources can be markers of change and progress if handled properly and peacefully.

Four kinds of resource conflict. At the wider scope, four kinds of resource conflict challenge national stability: (a) secessionist conflicts in which resource-rich regions seek to split away from the rest of a country; (b) disputes over resources as part of new national laws and conventions, for instance within a peace agreement or new constitution; (c) grievances over standalone projects such as mines and hydroelectric dams; and (d) cumulative impacts of multiple small-scale clashes, typically over land and livestock. Typically at the heart of these disputes are four contentious issues: ownership of the resources; allocation of power for managing access to or developing the resource; the distribution of resource revenues; and the environmental and social damage caused by extracting the resource.

Conflicts by resource. Water and pasture shortages cause conflicts in many areas: protests in Pakistan and Bolivia; conflicts in China (in the Shandong and Guangdong Provinces in 2000); Darfur (Sudan), where much of the fighting was due to water scarcity; between Nile riparian countries over the use of Nile water; pasture land conflict in Ethiopia between Somali and Afar pastoralists; and in Afghanistan, where village-level clashes in 2008 arose from the use of land and irrigation water. Bigger bodies of water serve fishing, transportation, development, offshore oilfields and culture, and could be sources of conflict if not handled wisely - fishing disputes led to the famous 'cod wars' between the UK and Iceland in the 1950s and 1970s, and the world's more than 263 shared watercourses are all potential sources of conflict. Land grants access to minerals, timber, animals, pasture and farm plots; people have strong emotional and symbolic attachments to it, but population growth and degradation make usable land scarce: Ecuador and Peru fought several wars over their disputed border; violent land conflict occurred recently in China, East Timor, Kosovo, Rwanda and Tajikistan; border conflicts and wars were waged between Ethiopia and Eritrea and between Ethiopia and Somalia; and border conflicts persist between India and Pakistan (over Kashmir) and between Ethiopia and Sudan.

Timber, fuel and conflict minerals. Timber grows scarcer with mounting populations; the textbook notes that today 46% of the 30% of world forest cover has been destroyed, and population growth and industrialization are destroying rainforests; examples of timber conflicts are available in Burma, Cambodia, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Liberia. Fuel scarcity, especially of petroleum, is a major concern: the world's largest reserves in Iran, Iraq, Nigeria, Venezuela and Sudan face ardent conflicts, and oil caused the Gulf war between Kuwait and Iraq in the Middle East and conflict between Cameroon and Nigeria in Africa. Precious stones become conflict minerals when their control and exploitation contribute to armed conflicts: diamonds in Western and Central Africa were used as income sources by rebel groups such as UNITA (the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola) and Sierra Leone's RUF (Revolutionary United Front) in the late 1990s, and by rebel groups in Liberia, Ivory Coast, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Republic of Congo; amber is cited in Russia and gold in Indonesia.

Conditions, forms, actors and settlement. Conflicts arise when user groups are excluded from participating in natural resource management; when resources are poorly managed and inequitably shared; when contradictions arise between local and introduced management systems; when confusion develops from absent information about government policy; when laws and policies contradict or lack clarity; when inequality in distribution exists; and when poor policy and unsuccessful program implementation prevail. Conflicts show themselves by breaking rules, by acts of sabotage and violence, sometimes as hidden or latent disputes, through grievances that rage because of fear, and by showing distrust. Actors range from local people in homesteads and neighboring communities over woodland, to villages, community-based organizations, domestic and multinational businesses, governments, international development agencies and NGOs. People generally rely on the same basic procedural modes: avoidance (acting to keep a conflict from becoming publicly acknowledged), coercion (threatening or using force to impose one's will), negotiation (a voluntary process in which parties reach agreement through consent), arbitration (submitting a conflict to a mutually agreeable third party who renders a decision), mediation (a third party facilitates negotiation but lacks the authority to impose a solution), and adjudication (relying on a judge or administrator to make a binding decision). The unit summary stresses that the remedy is equitable use, transparency and respect for the rights of others.

workedExamples.calculation: The residual range of 40-60% mirror-images the resource share, meaning resources are one of the two most powerful drivers in the period studied.
workedExamples.answer: Between about 40% and 60% of civil wars in the period had other - political, ethnic, ideological - root causes, but the resource share is remarkably high.

workedExamples.problem: Sort these events into the four kinds of resource conflict: a mineral region declaring independence in Africa; a community opposing a new dam; repeated villages fighting over a watering point; and a dispute over resource clauses in a new constitution.
workedExamples.given: The four kinds: secessionist; disputes over resources as part of new national laws (peace agreement, new constitution); grievances over standalone projects such as mines and dams; cumulative impacts of multiple small-scale clashes over land and livestock.
workedExamples.formula: Method: classify by the pattern of the dispute, not its resource.
workedExamples.substitution: Mineral region splitting away - secessionist; anti-dam protests - grievance over a standalone project; watering-point clashes - cumulative small-scale clashes; constitution clauses - dispute in new national conventions.
workedExamples.calculation: Each scenario matches one named kind without overlap.
workedExamples.answer: 1) Secessionist; 2) Standalone project grievance; 3) Cumulative small-scale clashes; 4) Dispute within new national conventions.

workedExamples.problem: Distinguish mediation from arbitration as ways of settling a pasture dispute between two pastoralist kebeles. Why would the textbook rank one of them better for durable peace?
workedExamples.given: Mediation: a third party facilitates negotiation but lacks the authority to impose a solution; Arbitration: the parties submit to a mutually agreeable third party who renders a decision; Negotiation: a voluntary process where parties agree by consent.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: consented agreements tend to endure because all stakeholders own them.
workedExamples.substitution: In mediation, elders or a neutral agency guide the talks but cannot force a verdict; in arbitration the third party decides for both.
workedExamples.calculation: Because mediation ends in a consented negotiation, both kebeles own the outcome and the sharing rule is more likely to hold - though arbitration is faster where trust is thin.
workedExamples.answer: Mediation guides but never imposes; arbitration decides for the parties. Mediation suits a resource both sides must share for years, since consented rules are kept longer.

workedExamples.problem: Diamonds became a rebel income source in Angola and Sierra Leone in the late 1990s. Explain the mechanism connecting reduced supply, rising price and conflict, and name one African state besides Angola and Sierra Leone from the example list.
workedExamples.given: The textbook: diamonds, minerals and natural oil are available in limited amounts; their market value rises when quantities shrink; when size shrinks, asset scarcity occurs and shortage triggers conflict.
workedExamples.formula: Concept: scarcity-price-conflict mechanism of exhaustible resources.
workedExamples.substitution: Fewer accessible diamond fields - higher world price - higher seizure value - armed groups (UNITA, RUF) fight for control.
workedExamples.calculation: Named states in the examples besides Angola and Sierra Leone are Liberia, Ivory Coast, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Republic of Congo.
workedExamples.answer: Rising scarcity raised the stones' value, making seizure profitable for armed groups; additional examples are Liberia, Ivory Coast, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Republic of Congo.

commonMistakes: Assuming scarcity alone always causes conflict; the textbook also shows grievances can be markers of change and progress when handled peacefully.
Confusing mediation and arbitration; the mediator facilitates but cannot impose, while the arbitrator renders a decision.
Forgetting conflicts can remain hidden or latent rather than always visible as violence.
Assuming resource conflicts concern only diamonds and oil; water, pasture, land, timber and fishing also trigger them.
Mixing up the Darfur and Kashmir examples: Darfur was about water scarcity; Kashmir is an India-Pakistan border conflict.
Believing conflict resolution is only courts and force; avoidance, negotiation, mediation and adjudication are all basic procedural modes.
Ignoring that recognizing conflict is a prerequisite for sustainable and equitable resource management.
applications: Reporting a water-point dispute in a school or kebele to elders and applying mediation rather than force.
Drafting equitable-use rules for a communal grazing land, applying the textbook's principles of transparency and respect for others' rights.
Analyzing the conflict between Somali and Afar pastoralists in Ethiopia as a case of resource pressure on pasture.
Tracing in a news article how oil contributed to conflict between Cameroon and Nigeria, then proposing prevention.
Checking whether a local shared forest has bylaws, joint monitoring and prior notification before extraction.
Teaching classmates why exchange of information and consultation between user groups reduce conflict risk.
g11-geography-ug3-t7.summary: Natural resource conflicts are disputes over accessing, controlling and using resources, triggered when exhaustible assets shrink and their value rises; some 40-60% of civil wars of the past six decades were instigated by resource control. Conflicts occur over water and pasture (Pakistan, Bolivia, Darfur, the Nile, Somali-Afar), land (Ecuador-Peru, Ethiopia-Eritrea), timber (Burma, Cambodia, DRC, Liberia) and fuel and minerals (Gulf war, Cameroon-Nigeria, UNITA and RUF diamonds). Settlement rests on equitable use, transparency and peaceful mechanisms such as negotiation, arbitration, mediation and adjudication.

config.title: Six Procedural Modes of Handling Conflict

steps.label: Avoidance
steps.detail: Acting in ways that keep a conflict from becoming publicly acknowledged.

steps.label: Coercion
steps.detail: Threatening or using force to impose one's will - risky and often harmful.

steps.label: Negotiation
steps.detail: A voluntary process in which parties reach agreement through consent.

steps.label: Arbitration
steps.detail: Submitting the dispute to a mutually agreeable third party who decides.

steps.label: Mediation
steps.detail: A third party facilitates negotiation but cannot impose a solution.

steps.label: Adjudication
steps.detail: Relying on a judge or administrator to make a binding decision.
